verses.translation_literal: Praise-Yah! Give thanks to YHWH, for [he is] good, for [is] for ever his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Lift up your voices and give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, and his steadfast love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the opening of a psalm that will go on to tell a long story of failure, and it begins with the same cry that ends Psalm 105 and Psalm 106 itself. 'Hallelu-Yah' is a plural command, 'all of you, praise Yah', so the actors are not alone: the line is spoken to a crowd. The KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' hides that it is one word in Hebrew, with the short divine name Yah inside it, and its 'mercy' renders chesed, which is not soft pity. Chesed is the loyalty one side of a covenant owes the other, and it is the reason the whole psalm can hold together. Say it as a refrain the congregation knows by heart; it is a liturgical formula (compare Ps 107:1; 118:1).

philological_notes.note: A plural imperative of halal 'to praise' with the short form of YHWH, one word in the text. Meaning 'all of you praise Yah'.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love; more than 'mercy'. Malbim reads it as the loyalty God keeps even after Israel sins.

verses.translation_literal: Who will speak the mighty deeds of YHWH, will cause to be heard all his praise?
verses.translation_dramatic: Who could ever tell the mighty deeds of the LORD? Who could make all his praise heard?
verses.directors_commentary: A question that expects the answer 'no one'. The speaker has just told the crowd to give thanks, and now admits that no language is large enough for the subject. The KJV's 'who can utter' is good; its 'shew forth' is archaic for 'cause to be heard', and the Hebrew verb is a hearing verb (yashmia', 'make hear'), not a showing one: praise is something spoken aloud, not displayed. The word gevurot, 'mighty deeds', is the vocabulary of military victory and will be exactly the subject of the story that follows, the Exodus. Give the line a pause before 'who', as if the speaker stops to take in the size of it. The mood is reverent, almost hushed, before the confession of verse 6.

philological_notes.note: Plural of gevurah, 'mighty deeds, acts of strength', typically in war; here the acts of God for Israel. Ibn Ezra ties them to the sea crossing.
A rare verb, 'to speak, utter', connected by Metzudat Zion to 'word' (milla).

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [are] the keepers of justice, [the] one doing righteousness at every time.
verses.translation_dramatic: Happy are those who keep to justice, happy the one who does what is right, in every season and at every hour.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns from praise to a wisdom saying, and a hard one: after admitting nobody can praise God enough, the speaker says who does come close, the people who live justly all the time. Notice the grammar. The 'keepers' are plural, but the 'one doing righteousness' is singular, as though the crowd suddenly becomes a single person. The KJV makes this smoother with 'they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness', which at least keeps the shift, but 'judgment' for mishpat is archaic: it means justice, the right order of a community, not a court verdict. 'Ashrei' is not 'blessed' in the sense of receiving a blessing; it is closer to 'oh, the happiness of', a congratulation. 'At every time' is the sting: Israel's story in this psalm is that they did it sometimes. Radak hears the whole psalm in these words, because Israel did right 'sometimes, and most of the time did wrong'.

philological_notes.note: An exclamation of congratulation, 'oh the happiness of', frequent at the start of Psalms (Ps 1:1). Not the same as barukh, 'blessed' by God.
Justice, right order, a judgment; here the ordinances of the Torah, as Metzudat David and Malbim read it.

verses.translation_literal: Remember me, YHWH, with the favour of your people; visit me with your salvation,
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember me, LORD, when you show your people favour. Come to me, and visit me with your rescue.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice becomes personal for the first time: 'me'. Two verbs, 'remember' and 'visit', are the language of a God who acts. To 'remember' in the Bible is to act on what one has in mind (Gen 8:1; Ex 2:24), and 'visit' (paqad) is to intervene, for good or for ill. Malbim notes that this is the point of the prayer: the speaker asks not to be visited for punishment, because the psalm is about to list exactly that. The KJV's 'favour that thou bearest unto thy people' smooths a phrase that is ambiguous in Hebrew, 'with the favour of your people'; it could mean the favour God has for them (so Rashi) or the favour they receive. Play the line quietly. The speaker is a small figure at the edge of a crowd, hoping to be counted in.

philological_notes.note: 'Visit me': paqad means to attend to, to intervene, with good or ill result. Metzudat Zion: 'providence and remembrance'. Malbim draws a difference between remembering and visiting.
'With the favour of your people', ambiguous: favour God shows them, or favour they enjoy. Rashi explains it as 'when you are pleased with your people'.

verses.translation_literal: to look on the good of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation, to boast with your inheritance.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let me see the good that comes to your chosen ones, share the gladness of your nation, and take pride beside the people who are your inheritance.
verses.directors_commentary: Three infinitives in a row, each saying what the speaker hopes for, and each in a different register: to look, to rejoice, to glory. They are one wish repeated in three ways, which Radak calls the habit of Hebrew poetry. Pay attention to the three names for Israel: 'chosen ones' (bachir, picked out), 'nation' (goy, the ordinary word for a people among peoples, sometimes used for the others), and 'inheritance' (nachalah, land and family property that one does not sell). Each says something different, belonging to God by choice, as a country, and as family property. The KJV's 'glory' for lehithallel is accurate but old: it is a reflexive, 'to make oneself praised', and in modern speech 'to boast'. The speaker wants to be able to say, with the others, 'we are the ones he chose', and that sets up the shock of the next verse, which admits why that boast has no basis.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of halal, 'to boast, glory', literally 'to make oneself praised'. Radak notes that some take it as 'rejoice' and prefers 'to be praised'.
Inheritance, family property held by God. Meiri cites Deut 9:29, 'they are your people and your inheritance'.

verses.translation_literal: We have sinned with our fathers; we have done wrong; we have acted wickedly.
verses.translation_dramatic: We have sinned, as our fathers sinned. We have twisted what was straight. We have done evil.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn of the whole psalm, in five words. Everything before was praise and hope; now comes confession, and it is in the first person plural: 'we'. The speaker does not blame the ancestors; he stands among them: 'with our fathers'. The KJV's 'we have committed iniquity' stays close to the Hebrew, but the three verbs are chosen to escalate: chata' (miss the mark), 'avah (to bend, to twist), rasha' (to be guilty, to act as a wicked person). Say them as a descending staircase, each heavier than the one before. The same triad appears in Solomon's temple prayer (1 Kings 8:47) and in Daniel 9:5, which suggests a standard liturgy of confession. The speaker is a later generation, probably in exile (Radak: 'he speaks in the voice of the exile'), and what makes the psalm unusual is that the confession is a recital of history, not a private cry.

philological_notes.note: From 'avah, 'to bend, to make crooked', hence 'to act perversely'. Ibn Ezra notes that the verb lacks an object and is read as intransitive.
'With our fathers': the speaker joins himself to the earlier generations, as Radak and Metzudat David explain, 'as our fathers sinned, so we sinned'.

verses.translation_literal: Our fathers in Egypt did not consider your wonders; they did not remember the abundance of your covenant loyalties, and they rebelled at [the] sea, at the Sea of Reeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our fathers, in Egypt itself, did not take in your wonders. They did not remember how great were your faithful acts. And at the sea, at the Sea of Reeds, they rebelled.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the story starts, and it starts with a failure of attention. The Hebrew says the fathers 'did not consider' (lo hiskilu) the wonders: the verb, in its causative form, means to act with insight, to draw the right conclusion. They saw the plagues and did not understand what they meant. The second verb is memory: 'they did not remember' the 'abundance' of God's chasadim, plural, as many separate acts of loyalty. Then the verb vayamru, 'they rebelled', and the setting repeated twice in a way that tolerates the idea of a place with a name: 'at sea, at the Sea of Reeds'. The KJV's 'provoked him' adds a pronoun that is not in the Hebrew and treats the verb as causing anger, whereas it says plainly that they rebelled. And 'Red sea' is a tradition from the Greek translation; the Hebrew is Yam Suf, the sea of reeds. Rashi and Metzudat David both fill the scene: the people at the shore said that as they came up one side, the Egyptians would come up the other and chase them (compare Ex 14:11).

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of sakhal: to understand, to act with insight. Not merely to know, but to draw the right conclusion. Metzudat David: 'they did not set their heart to understand'.
'They rebelled', from marah, to be refractory, to defy. The KJV 'provoked him' reads the verb with an object that the Hebrew does not give. Metzudat Zion: 'they rebelled and refused'.
'Sea of Reeds'. Suf is a word for reeds (borrowed from Egyptian). The KJV 'Red sea' follows the Greek and Latin tradition.

verses.translation_literal: And he saved them for the sake of his name, to make known his might.
verses.translation_dramatic: Yet he saved them, for the sake of his own name, so that his power would be known.
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the surprise of the psalm: God saves a people who have just been described as rebels. The reason is not their merit but 'his name', meaning his reputation among the nations. In the ancient Near East, a god who could not protect his own people was a god who had been beaten, and the Egyptians would have said so; Metzudat David puts this plainly: the saving was so that the name would not be profaned. The KJV's 'Nevertheless' is a good reading of the Hebrew 'and', which here marks a sharp contrast, even though the word itself is plain. 'To make known his might' echoes Ex 14:4, 17-18, where God says he will gain glory over Pharaoh so that Egypt will know. Deliver it as a reversal: the voice has just been sinking, and now it rises, though the reason it gives is not flattering to Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'For the sake of his name': God's name is his standing and reputation. Malbim ties it to Ezek 20, where God acts so that his name will not be profaned.

verses.translation_literal: And he rebuked the Sea of Reeds, and it dried up, and he led them in the deeps like the wilderness.
verses.translation_dramatic: He rebuked the Sea of Reeds, and it dried up. He led them down through the deeps as if across the open wilderness.
verses.directors_commentary: The sea is treated here as a hostile power that can be shouted at, as God shouts at the chaos waters in Ps 18:15 and 104:7. The verb ga'ar, 'rebuke', is the word for talking down a wild animal or a disorderly army, and it makes the Exodus into a small battle with the sea itself. That is a polemic against the idea, known from Canaanite and Mesopotamian myth, that the sea is a god who must be fought: here it is a subordinate that obeys a word. The KJV's 'He rebuked the Red sea also' adds 'also', which is not there, and 'through the depths, as through the wilderness' softens the picture, because the Hebrew has the people walking 'in the deeps', that is, on the floor of the deep, as if the deeps were a wilderness. Tehom is the primeval deep of Gen 1:2, so the line is almost a creation image. Isa 63:13 uses the same words ('led them through the deeps, like a horse in the wilderness'). Speak it slowly, with space for the sound of the sea going quiet.

philological_notes.note: 'And he rebuked': the verb for a forceful reprimand, used of God subduing the waters. Radak explains the rebuke as the wind that dried the sea; Ibn Ezra likens the east wind to a rebuke.
Plural of tehom, 'the deep', the primeval waters of Gen 1:2; here the sea floor. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'low places'.

verses.translation_literal: And he saved them from the hand of [one who] hated, and he redeemed them from the hand of [an] enemy.
verses.translation_dramatic: He saved them from the hand of the one who hated them, and bought them back from the grip of the enemy.
verses.directors_commentary: A parallel couplet in which the two lines say the same thing with two verbs and two names for the enemy. 'Saved' (yosha') and 'redeemed' (ga'al) are not the same: ga'al is the word for a family member who buys back a relative from slavery or debt, and it gives the Exodus a family colour, God as the kinsman who pays the price. 'Hand' stands for power, so 'from the hand of' means 'out of the power of'. The 'one who hated' is, as Ibn Ezra says, Pharaoh. The KJV adds 'him that hated them' and so makes the participle a plain person; the Hebrew is a bare participle, 'a hater', as 'an enemy' in the second line is. Malbim notes that 'enemy' is more open in its hostility than 'hater'. Take this verse as a breath between the miracle of verse 9 and the drowning of verse 11.

philological_notes.note: 'And he redeemed them': the kinsman-redeemer verb, to buy back a relative from slavery or loss (Lev 25:48). Malbim reads it as a more lasting freedom than 'saved'.

verses.translation_literal: And water covered their opponents; one of them was not left.
verses.translation_dramatic: The waters closed over their pursuers, and not one of them was left.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn from rescue to judgment is one short sentence. The same sea that stood open for Israel closes on the Egyptians, and the writer says nothing more. 'Water' is plural in Hebrew (mayim) as always; the sentence has no 'the' before it, so it is bare 'waters', and this is how the text of Ex 15:5 and 10 describes them, covering like a garment. 'Their opponents' (tzareihem) is a stronger word than the previous verse's 'enemy': tzar is the one who presses you into a corner, from the root meaning 'narrow', and Malbim says that the tzar fights actively. The KJV's 'enemies' flattens that. The last clause, 'not one of them was left' is a deliberate echo of Ex 14:28, 'not so much as one of them remained'. Keep the voice flat, not triumphant: the text states the fact without celebration.

philological_notes.note: 'Their opponents': from tzarar, to bind, to press in, so the one who presses. Malbim: the tzar actually fights and oppresses, unlike the enemy who only wishes harm.
'Not one was left', echoing Ex 14:28, 'not one of them remained'.

verses.translation_literal: And they believed in his words; they sang his praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then they believed his words, and they sang his praise.
verses.directors_commentary: The first half of the psalm ends with a hopeful verse, and the commentators all hear Exodus in it: 'and they believed in the LORD' (Ex 14:31) and 'then Moses sang' (Ex 15:1). Meiri, Malbim and Ibn Ezra each draw the same lines. The verb ya'aminu is built on the root 'aman, 'to be firm, to trust', and the preposition bet gives 'they believed in his words', a trust that rests on something. The KJV's 'Then believed they his words' rightly gets the 'then', but its word order is archaic and loses the weight that the narrator gives to the new trust. And 'they sang' (yashiru) is a vividly short verb: the song of the sea is one of the oldest poems in the Bible. The sting is in the contrast: Israel believed only after they saw, and the next verses (13-14) begin with the words 'they quickly forgot'. Play this as a brief clear light, which the audience knows will not last.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'aman, 'to be firm, trustworthy': to believe, to put one's trust in. Meiri and Malbim connect it to Ex 14:31.
'They sang': Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as the Song at the Sea (Ex 15:1).

verses.translation_literal: They hurried; they forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel.
verses.translation_dramatic: But how swiftly it faded. The sea was barely dry on their sandals, and already the wonders were gone from their minds. They would not wait. They would not stand still and listen for what the LORD intended.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speed is the point. Hebrew has no connecting word between 'they hurried' and 'they forgot': the two verbs fall one on the other, like a stumble. The tradition ties this to the three days from the Sea to Marah, when the people complained about bitter water (Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David on this verse, citing Exodus 15). A desert traveller then lived by water; three days without it was a crisis, so the anger is easy to understand, and the Psalm judges it anyway.

The KJV 'they soon forgat' turns the first verb into an adverb and loses the double beat. 'Waited not for his counsel' is sound, but 'wait' (חכה) here is active hope, a posture of expectancy, not idle delay (Metzudat Zion compares Zephaniah 3:8). And 'counsel' (עצה) is a plan, not advice that can be shrugged off: it is what the LORD was already in the middle of doing. Actors should play impatience as the opposite of trust, not as simple bad temper.

philological_notes.note: 'They hurried': a verb of haste standing alone, placed first so that it sets the pace of the verse. English translations usually bend it into 'soon' and lose the verb.
To wait expectantly for something. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'a sense of waiting' and compares Zephaniah 3:8.
God's plan or purpose. Radak and Metzudat David say that this plan was good: the bitter water was in fact about to be sweetened.

verses.translation_literal: And they craved a craving in the wilderness, and they tested God in the desolation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hunger, then, became appetite, and appetite became a fever. In the wilderness they craved, they craved with their whole mouth, and out in that barren emptiness they put God himself to the test.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew uses a figure that English finds clumsy: 'they craved a craving' (ויתאוו תאוה), the verb and its own noun together. It is meant to sound like appetite feeding on itself. The KJV's 'lusted exceedingly' captures the intensity but hides the wordplay; the Hebrew does not say 'exceedingly', it says the craving was the whole substance of the act.

The background is Numbers 11:4: 'Who will feed us meat?' (Rashi and Metzudat David both point there). They had manna, but they wanted meat and fish, the tastes of Egypt. Radak and Meiri read the second verb as the real sin: they were not just hungry, they were asking whether God was able to supply meat in a desert (נסה, 'test, try'). The KJV's 'tempted' is a seventeenth-century word for 'tried' and now misleads, because it suggests that God was being enticed. The last word, ישימון, is 'a desolation', a place without any life; the Psalm chooses it to underline what they were demanding of such a place.

philological_notes.note: A verb with its own cognate noun: 'they craved a craving'. Rashi identifies the craving as the request for meat in Numbers 11:4.
To put to the test. Radak and Meiri say that the test was whether God could provide meat in the wilderness. KJV 'tempted' is archaic for 'tested'.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave to them their petition, and he sent a wasting into their throat-self.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he gave it. Everything they had asked for, he gave. But with the gift he sent something else, a wasting that crept into the very life of them, and the feast became a sickness.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse where the story turns. 'He gave them their request' sounds like generosity, but the second clause overturns it. In Numbers 11:33 the meat was still between their teeth when the plague struck (Rashi cites that verse), and the place was named for it: the graves of craving. The Psalm withholds the place-name and gives only the irony.

The key word is רזון, 'leanness' in the KJV, 'a wasting disease' in the BBE. Radak and Ibn Ezra say it means the death of those who craved: they had wanted to be filled and fattened, and the result was the opposite. Metzudat David reads it more literally, as thinness: the quail did not fatten them. The Hebrew allows both and I have left it open. And נפש, here 'soul' in the KJV, is not the Greek or modern soul. It is the self, the throat, the appetite. The craving lived in the nefesh, so the wasting is sent there. 'Into their soul' in English suggests a spiritual affliction; the Hebrew is bodily and total.

philological_notes.note: Thinness, wasting. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as the death of the craving ones; Metzudat David as literal thinning. The word turns the expectation of being fattened upside down.
'Their self, their throat, their appetite.' The seat of the craving, which is where the wasting is sent.

verses.translation_literal: And they were jealous of Moses in the camp, of Aaron, the holy one of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, inside the camp itself, among the tents and the cooking smoke, they turned on Moses. They turned on Aaron, too, the man set apart for the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene moves from the desert to the camp: this is rebellion at home. It points to the revolt of Korah, Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16), which Radak and Meiri identify here. Their slogan was 'all the congregation are holy' (Numbers 16:3), and Radak explains the title 'holy one of the LORD' as Moses's answer: the holy one is the one whom the LORD chooses.

The KJV's 'saint' misleads. Today it suggests personal piety; the Hebrew קדוש means set apart, which is a status, here the priestly office. The verb is also tricky. קנא can be zeal or jealousy, and it normally takes ב for hostility, but here it takes ל. Radak and Meiri discuss the shift: the lamed may stand for bet ('they envied Moses'), or the verb may mean 'they provoked' as in Deuteronomy 32:21 (Rashi). I have used 'jealous of', and the KJV 'envied' is fine. The KJV's 'also' is not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: Jealousy, envy, provocation. The usual preposition for hostile envy is bet; here it is lamed, which Radak and Meiri read as equivalent to bet, and Rashi connects to the 'provoking' sense of Deuteronomy 32:21.
'The holy one of YHWH', Aaron as the one set apart. Ibn Ezra links it to the Levites and Numbers 16:5; Radak to the claim that all the congregation were holy.

verses.translation_literal: The earth opened, and it swallowed Dathan, and it covered over the company of Abiram.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the ground answered. It opened. It swallowed Dathan whole, and then it closed above the whole company of Abiram, and there was only earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
No speech, no warning in the Psalm: just the ground. In Numbers 16:31-33 the earth split under the tents of Dathan and Abiram and closed over them. The poet leaves out Korah, the instigator. Rashi suggests the poet spared Korah's sons the mention of their father and blamed Dathan and Abiram instead; Radak adds that it names the helpers because helpers in wickedness share the guilt, and that On son of Pelet repented and fell silent.

The verb forms are a puzzle for translators. The first, תפתח, is imperfect, yet the story is past; Ibn Ezra calls it a 'standing' time, and Radak 'future in the place of past'. This is common in Hebrew poetry and the KJV rightly renders it as a past. Two verbs, 'swallowed' and 'covered', give the sense of a mouth closing, and עדה, 'company', includes families (Ibn Ezra: their wives and children).

philological_notes.note: An imperfect with a past sense, common in poetry. Radak: 'future in the place of past'.
'The company of Abiram'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the households: they, their wives and their little ones.

verses.translation_literal: And fire burned in their company; a flame set the wicked ablaze.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then fire. It broke out in their midst and ran through them, and the flame fed on the wicked.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two judgments in two verses, earth then fire, and the second is told in a parallel pair of lines: 'fire burned' and 'flame set ablaze'. Radak notes that the verse repeats itself in different words; this is Hebrew parallelism, and it makes the fire audible, a rolling, doubled crackle.

The fire is the one of Numbers 16:35 that consumed the 250 men offering incense (Rashi, Meiri, Radak). The KJV 'a fire was kindled' makes it passive and distant; the Hebrew has the fire itself as the subject. 'The wicked' is a general word (רשעים) and not a name: the Psalm turns specific men into a type. The verb להט is a rarer one for burning, used of flames that lick and scorch.

philological_notes.note: 'Sets ablaze, licks up'. Metzudat Zion says it is connected with the idea of the flame. The imperfect has a past meaning, as Meiri says of all these verbs.

verses.translation_literal: They make a calf at Horeb, and they bow down to a molten image.
verses.translation_dramatic: At Horeb, at the very mountain where the voice had spoken, they made a calf. They made it, and they bowed down to the thing they had poured out of metal.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem jumps back in time. Horeb is Sinai, and the calf (Exodus 32) happened before Korah's revolt; Meiri and Malbim both remark on the order. The point of the place name is the shock: at the mountain where the Ten Commandments were heard, with 'you shall not make for yourself an idol' and 'you shall not bow down' (Radak, Meiri).

The verb is in the imperfect, as Radak says, 'future in the place of past'. The KJV 'worshipped' is a good rendering of השתחוה, but literally it is 'bent oneself low', a bodily act. English readers hear 'calf' as small and cute; עגל is a young bull, a symbol of strength and fertility, and in Egyptian and Canaanite art a throne or pedestal for a deity. 'Molten image' (מסכה) is a cast piece of metal, so the Psalm insists on its manufactured nature.

philological_notes.note: Horeb, the other name of the mountain of the law. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all stress that this was where they had received the law and heard the voice.
A poured or cast image. Metzudat Zion: something melted from metal, as in 'gods of metal' (Exodus 34).

verses.translation_literal: And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of an ox, an eater of grass.
verses.translation_dramatic: They traded their glory. They traded it away for the shape of an ox, a beast that stands in a field and chews grass.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the Psalm's sharpest line, and it is sarcasm. 'They exchanged' is the language of a market: they swapped. What they gave up was 'their glory', and the commentators take that to mean God himself, the glory they had seen on the mountain (Radak, Metzudat David: 'the glory of the Place'); Ibn Ezra reads it as a euphemistic title for God. What they took in return was 'an ox that eats grass'.

The last two words are not decoration. The KJV's 'an ox that eateth grass' preserves them but not the sting: Ibn Ezra says they are said 'in contempt and disgrace', Metzudat David that the ox soils the grass with its saliva as it eats, and Rashi quotes the Mekhilta that nothing is more revolting than an ox eating. The audience should hear scorn. Compare the contemptuous mockery of idol-makers elsewhere in the Bible.

philological_notes.note: To exchange, trade one thing for another. Metzudat Zion: a word of substitution and replacement.
'Eater of herbage': added as a mocking description of the idol. Ibn Ezra reads it as contempt; Rashi quotes the Mekhilta for the revulsion at an ox chewing.

verses.translation_literal: They forgot God, their deliverer, doer of great things in Egypt,
verses.translation_dramatic: They forgot God. They forgot the one who had pulled them out, the one who had done great things in Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb of v.13 returns: 'they forgot' (שכחו). Here the forgetting has an object and a title, 'God their deliverer', literally 'their saving one'. The KJV 'saviour' is not wrong, but in English it now has Christian overtones; the Hebrew מושיע is a rescuer from danger, an ordinary word for the one who pulls you out. The participle 'doer' (עשה) is present-tense, as though his deeds were still his description.

The cause is time: Ibn Ezra says that the Exodus was so recent that the forgetting is outrageous. The sentence is not finished: it runs on into v.22, and the great things of Egypt are named only there. Director's note: the list should be delivered as a reproach, not as history.

philological_notes.note: 'Their deliverer', one who rescues. Ibn Ezra connects it to the Sea of Reeds, which was only just behind them.

verses.translation_literal: Wonders in the land of Ham, awesome deeds at the Sea of Reeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wonders in the land of Ham. Terrible, awesome things at the Sea of Reeds.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two halves of the verse set the two scenes side by side: the plagues in Egypt and the crossing of the sea. Both lines are short, with no verb, so that they land like a list of what was forgotten.

The KJV 'Red sea' comes from the Greek translation; the Hebrew is יַם־סוּף, literally 'Sea of Reeds'. 'The land of Ham' is a poetic name for Egypt: Radak notes that Ham was the father of Mizraim, the Hebrew name of Egypt (Genesis 10:6). The second adjective, נוראות, is the KJV 'terrible', which in 1611 meant 'inspiring terror' and now sounds like 'awful'. Radak says the deeds are 'awesome' because through them people fear the LORD, who overturns nature at will.

philological_notes.note: A poetic name for Egypt. Radak says Ham was the father of Egypt (Mizraim).
'Sea of Reeds', which the Greek translation and the KJV render 'Red Sea'. The traditional name is a translation tradition, not a literal rendering.
'Fearsome, awe-inspiring deeds'. Radak: they are awesome because they make people fear the LORD, who reverses nature at will.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to destroy them — had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn back his wrath from destroying.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the word was spoken: they will be destroyed. Destroyed, and nothing left. But one man stood in the broken wall, his chosen one, Moses, standing there before the face of God. He stood, and the fury turned back. It turned back from the ruin.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse hangs on a half-finished sentence. "He said to destroy them" is the decree, and the "unless" (לוּלֵי) arrives only in the next breath, so the audience must feel the sentence fall before it is caught. Ibn Ezra reads the saying as the words of Deut 9:14, "Let me alone, that I may destroy them," and Meiri ties the rescue to Exod 32:11-14. Malbim adds that God's "let me alone" is what showed Moses the matter depended on him.

The image is military and civic: a breach (פֶּרֶץ) is a gap in a city wall or a field's fence. An attacker pours through a breach, so a defender must stand in it with his own body. Radak says Moses stood in the very gap God had made, and Metzudat David says it is a comparison to one standing where the fence is broken to bar the way in. Moses defends Israel not against an enemy but against God himself, and he does it with prayer, not a sword. Note the word בְּחִירוֹ, "his chosen one." In v.5 the psalm used the same root for the whole people (בְּחִירֶיךָ, "your chosen ones"); here it gives the word to one man, Moses, who stands in for them. The same word is used of David in Ps 89:4, so the title is the language of covenant and election, not of rank.

The KJV runs the verse together: "Therefore he said that he would destroy them" adds "that he would," and "lest he should destroy them" turns a plain "from destroying" into a purpose clause with an archaic "lest." It also supplies "Therefore," which the Hebrew does not have. The Hebrew has an infinitive, "to destroy," and then the identical root again, "from destroying" (מֵהַשְׁחִית), so the decree and its cancellation are one word at both ends. Hold that echo.

philological_notes.note: A breach or gap, as in a wall. The same root returns in v.29 for the plague that "broke out" (וַתִּפְרָץ) among the people. Moses stands in a gap, as the plague had burst through one.
"His chosen one." The psalm used the plural for Israel as a whole in v.5 (בְּחִירֶיךָ) and gives it here to Moses, one man who stands for them. Compare Ps 89:4 for David.

"To destroy them," a Hiphil infinitive that means exterminate. It is paired with מֵהַשְׁחִית, "from destroying," at the verse's end, a different root with the same sense, so the verse begins and ends on destruction.

verses.translation_literal: And they rejected the land of desire; they did not believe his word.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then they spurned the land, the desired land. They would not believe what he had said.
verses.directors_commentary:
The next episode is the spies (Numbers 13-14). Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat David all say so: after the report of the spies the people rejected the land. Ibn Ezra puts it at the departure from Horeb. The Psalm's verdict is two-fold: they despised the land, and they did not believe the word.

The verb מאס is stronger than 'despise': it is to reject something as worthless, to throw it away. YLT 'kick against' is vivid but not literal. 'Land of desire' (ארץ חמדה) is the opposite of the craving of v.14: the people craved meat, but they had no desire for the land that had been promised to them. The KJV 'pleasant land' is gentle. Then 'they believed not his word' uses the same verb, האמין, that is used of Abraham (Genesis 15:6); to believe is to rely, to trust that the speaker is firm, and the failure to do so is the real crime.

philological_notes.note: 'A desirable land', the land of Canaan. It is the counterpart to the 'craving' of v.14: they craved what they could not have and rejected the one thing that was promised.
'To believe, to trust'. Meiri says it means they did not trust the word enough to go up and fight, and that they sent spies first, at their own request (Deuteronomy 1:22).

verses.translation_literal: And they murmured in their tents; they did not listen to the voice of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the grumbling went on behind the tent-flaps. Low voices, close and bitter, passed from one doorway to the next, while the voice of the LORD went out over the camp and found no ear willing to take it in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is the camp at the edge of the land, after the spies' report (Numbers 14, echoing Deuteronomy 1:27, "you murmured in your tents"). Nobody here shouts. The complaint is whispered indoors, among family, where no one has to answer for it, and that is exactly the point: the psalm calls it disobedience, because to refuse to listen is to refuse the voice. Play it as muttering, not rebellion.

The KJV "murmured" is fair, but BBE "talking against him secretly" shows what the Hebrew verb carries: רגן is the sound of a whisperer. The same root gives the "talebearer" (נרגן) of Proverbs, as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion note. The second clause is the blunt verdict: "did not listen" is the Hebrew idiom for "did not obey", the same verb שמע for hearing and obeying.

philological_notes.note: To murmur or grumble, from the whisperer's grumbling; the noun נרגן is the slanderer or complainer. The niphal reflexive suggests grumbling among themselves.
'Listen to the voice of' is the covenant idiom for obey; the hearing is not in doubt, the response is.

verses.translation_literal: And he lifted his hand to them, to make them fall in the wilderness,
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD raised his hand. It was no blow but a vow, sworn in the open air before the whole camp: that in that wilderness, and nowhere else, they would fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
To lift the hand is to swear. A man in the ancient world raised his hand toward heaven to bind himself by oath, and the commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, the Targum) all read the phrase so. The KJV "lifted up his hand against them" keeps the gesture but adds "against", which makes it sound like a raised fist; the Hebrew says "to them", and the ASV "sware unto them" and BBE "made an oath" are closer to what the gesture means. God's raised hand here is the grave counterpart of the raised hand of promise at the Exodus.

The verb "to make fall" is vivid: the generation dies in the open desert, as Numbers 14 has it, where their bodies would "fall". The KJV "overthrow" is a battle word and loses the plain image of the dead lying where they dropped. The same verb comes back in verse 27.

philological_notes.note: 'Lifted his hand': the oath gesture. The psalm compresses Numbers 14 and the wording of Ezekiel 20.
Hiphil of 'fall': to cause to fall. It is used for death by judgment, here the generation dying in the wilderness.

verses.translation_literal: and to make their seed fall among the nations, and to scatter them in the lands.
verses.translation_dramatic: And that their children, too, should fall, but far from here, among the nations; and that they should be scattered like seed flung wide over strange lands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The oath reaches past the generation that died: now their descendants are in view, falling among the nations and scattered abroad. The verse is a sudden widening of time, from one wilderness to many lands, and the actors should let the voice drop and lengthen on it. Rashi hears the destruction of the Temple here (the night they wept, the ninth of Av, a weeping fixed for the generations), and Radak notes that the Torah does not state this oath in these words but that Ezekiel 20:23 does.

The KJV "overthrow" again covers the verb "make fall", which the Hebrew repeats from verse 26 for the second half of the oath. "Scatter" is a farmer's word, a fanning of grain (Metzudat Zion compares Ezekiel 5), and the KJV "in the lands" is right to keep the plural, which is the world beyond the promised one.

philological_notes.note: To scatter or winnow, as grain is thrown to the wind; here, the dispersal of a people.

verses.translation_literal: And they yoked themselves to Baal of Peor, and they ate sacrifices of the dead.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, at Peor, they bound themselves to Baal, and sat down to eat at the tables of the dead.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene moves to Shittim, to the cult of Baal at Peor (Numbers 25), where the people were first drawn in by invitation to a sacrificial meal. The Hebrew verb "yoked themselves" is from the word for a pair of oxen: they let themselves be hitched to the god like animals to a plough. The KJV "joined themselves" is accurate but pale; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion hear joining and fastening, a lasting bond (as in a sealed cord).

"Sacrifices of the dead" is a barbed phrase. Radak and Metzudat David read it as sacrifices to lifeless gods, an insult to the idols; the other reading is offerings in honor of the dead. The KJV leaves it literal, and so should the actors, with a chill on "dead".

philological_notes.note: To be yoked or coupled, from the pair of draught animals; used for the people's attachment to the Baal of Peor in Numbers 25:3.
Either sacrifices offered to lifeless gods or offerings to the dead; the phrase is deliberately insulting to the cult.

verses.translation_literal: And they provoked [him] to anger by their deeds, and a plague broke out among them.
verses.translation_dramatic: So they stirred his anger with what they did, and a plague burst upon them, breaking through like water through a wall.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse gives a quick cause and effect: deeds, anger, plague. The word "deeds" is neutral in Hebrew, simply what they did, where the KJV "inventions" is a stretch, as if the people had made something new; the sense is their doings, and the ASV "doings" is closer. "Provoked" is the verb for angering, and the object (God) is understood, not stated.

The verb "broke out" is a breach: the plague broke through a wall, a flood through a dam. Metzudat Zion hears strength in it, Meiri a great breach in the people. Numbers 25:9 counts twenty-four thousand dead. Play it as a sudden break after the long slow whisper of verse 25.

philological_notes.note: 'Deeds' or 'doings', often with a bad sense; the KJV 'inventions' adds an idea of contrivance that the word does not carry.
To break out or burst through a barrier; here of the plague bursting among them.

verses.translation_literal: And Phinehas stood up and intervened as judge, and the plague was restrained.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Phinehas stood. One man rose where all the rest were falling, and he acted; and the plague, which no one else could hold, was held.
verses.directors_commentary:
Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, is the one who stands while everyone else is struck down. The verb ויפלל is the crux. Most of the classical commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion) connect it to פְּלִילִים, judgments, and read "he executed judgment" on Zimri and the Midianite woman in Numbers 25; the KJV follows them. BBE and the Targum read "he prayed", from the usual sense of the verb in the hithpael. The text does not mention the spear, and the actors should not add it: it says only that he stood, acted, and the plague stopped.

The final verb is passive and quiet: the plague "was restrained", held back as a gate is shut. The same sense is in Numbers 25:8. The KJV "so" adds a link that the Hebrew simply states by the plain "and".

philological_notes.note: Disputed: 'he judged, gave a verdict' (from פְּלִילִים, as in Exodus 21:22) or 'he prayed, interceded'. The commentators in the packet take the first sense.
To be held back, shut up, restrained; a word of stopping and prevention.

verses.translation_literal: And it was reckoned to him as righteousness, to a generation and a generation, until perpetuity.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it was written to his account as righteousness: from one generation to the next, to the farthest reach of time.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reward, and the language is the language of accounting: "it was reckoned to him". The Hebrew uses the same verb and the same noun, "reckoned" and "righteousness", as Genesis 15:6 for Abraham; the audience would hear that echo. The KJV "counted unto him for righteousness" is accurate; the BBE paraphrase, that later generations "kept the memory" of it, changes who does the reckoning.

The lasting reward is the covenant of priesthood (Numbers 25:12-13), as Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David note. "From generation to generation" is literally "to a generation and a generation", an idiom of repetition, and "perpetuity" (עולם) is the long unbounded time, which the KJV renders "for evermore".

philological_notes.note: 'It was reckoned to him as righteousness': the verb of accounting, as in Genesis 15:6. The deed is entered as a credit and is not merely approved.

verses.translation_literal: And they made [him] angry at the waters of Meribah, and it went badly for Moses because of them,
verses.translation_dramatic: And again they roused his anger, at the waters of Meribah, the waters of quarrel; and Moses paid for it. Evil came upon him because of them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm moves back to the wilderness, to Meribah (Numbers 20), where the people quarrelled over water. The name means "quarrel, contention": the KJV translates it, "waters of strife", while the ASV and BBE keep the name. The actors should hear that the waters are named after the quarrel. The verb "made angry" is a stronger word for wrath than the "provoked to anger" of verse 29.

The focus is on Moses. "It went badly for Moses" is literally "it was evil to Moses": the same root as "evil", used for what happened to him, namely that he was shut out of the land. Metzudat David and Radak read it just so. The KJV "went ill with Moses" is good; the blame is placed on the people ("because of them"), as in Deuteronomy 1:37.

philological_notes.note: 'Waters of Meribah', named for the quarrel (ריב) there; Ibn Ezra specifies Meribah of Kadesh.
'It was bad for Moses': the harm that fell on him, which the commentators identify as the decree that he would not enter the land.

verses.translation_literal: For they rebelled against his spirit, and he spoke rashly with his lips.
verses.translation_dramatic: They pushed against his spirit until it broke. And words slipped from his lips, rash words, words he could never call back.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the shortest verse of the window and the hardest to cast, because the Hebrew never says whose spirit it is or who speaks. Three suspects stand in the dock: Israel, Moses, and God. The scene is Num 20, with a thirsty people at Meribah, and the director must choose a reading before the actors can move.

The reading most singers hear is that Israel rebelled and Moses, worn down, spoke rashly: Metzudat David has Moses calling them "rebels" ("Hear now, you rebels", Num 20:10), and Meiri's first reading is that the people so angered Moses' spirit that his anger made him say what he should not. Radak's first comment agrees, adding that Moses and Aaron said "Shall we bring water out of this rock?", taking the credit for themselves. Rashi reads the subject differently: Moses and Aaron are the ones who rebelled against God's spirit, with "Hear now, you rebels" as the offense, and the "speaking" is God's oath, "Therefore you shall not bring this assembly" (Num 20:12). Radak's second comment and Ibn Ezra also read the speaking as God's, a decree that Moses would not enter the land; Ibn Ezra even offers the spirit as God's own, as in Isa 63:10, and still allows Moses' spirit. Meiri gives the same pair of options. So the verse can mean "Israel embittered Moses and he blurted" or "they rebelled against God's spirit and God pronounced." The dramatic layer follows the first.

The verb הִמְרוּ is from מָרָה, "to rebel, be defiant." Metzudat Zion glosses it "rebelled and refused." It is the same verb the psalm used in v.7 and v.43, so a listener should hear this as another round of the old pattern. The BBE has "made his spirit bitter," a legitimate alternative that plays on the sound of מַר, "bitter," but the psalm's own usage favors "rebelled." The KJV and Webster say "provoked," which blurs rebellion into irritation and makes the people merely annoying. The ASV's "were rebellious against" is closer.

וַיְבַטֵּא means to speak thoughtlessly, an utterance that escapes before judgment. The KJV's "spake unadvisedly" is accurate, if archaic. The ancient audience would hear that even the most faithful man of the whole story could speak a word he could not retract, and that one word cost him the land.

philological_notes.note: "They rebelled against." The same root as וַיַּמְרוּ in v.7 and יַמְרוּ in v.43, so it is kept as "rebelled" throughout. BBE's "made bitter" is a possible alternative, but this is not the usual sense of the verb in the psalm. Metzudat Zion glosses it "rebelled and refused."

"His spirit." It may be God's spirit (Ibn Ezra with Isa 63:10; Radak's second reading; Meiri) or Moses' spirit (Radak's first comment; Meiri). Metzudat Zion takes רוח as "speech," as in "the breath of his lips" (Isa 11:4).
"And he spoke rashly": to blurt out. Metzudat Zion links it to Lev 5:4, "to speak rashly with the lips." Rashi reads it as an oath, God's "you shall not bring this assembly."

verses.translation_literal: They did not destroy the peoples, of whom YHWH had said to them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not destroy the peoples, though the LORD had spoken plainly: that is what he said to them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now leaps across the desert into the land itself. The failing is one of omission: the instructions were to drive out or destroy the peoples of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7, 20:16-18), and Israel left them in place. Rashi refers to Judges 1:27 where they were set to forced labor instead of being removed. Meiri adds that the peoples were left and then mixed with.

The Hebrew is more clipped than the KJV: "which YHWH said to them", with the content left implied, where the KJV "commanded" turns a statement into a command, which is a fair guess at its force. The verb "destroy" (שמד) is the harsh verb of extermination, and the actors should hear that the people are accused of mercy where the God of the story demanded severity. Note, too, that the speaker of the psalm treats this as sin without softening.

philological_notes.note: To destroy utterly, to exterminate; the verb of the ban against the peoples of the land.

verses.translation_literal: And they mixed themselves with the nations, and they learned their deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: They did not keep apart. They mingled with the nations until the lines between them blurred, and in that closeness they learned, step by step, to do as the nations did.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is two beats, and the second follows from the first. First comes the mixing, then the learning. Radak reads it that way: they lived among the peoples, and so they learned their ways. Nothing here is a sudden apostasy. It is the slow effect of sharing a village, a market and a table. The previous verse said Israel did not destroy the peoples; this verse shows what that left behind.

Play the first half quietly and the second half with a chill. The KJV's "mingled among the heathen" does catch the sense, but "heathen" is a loaded, archaic word. The Hebrew says only בַּגּוֹיִם, "with the nations", plain peoples with their own customs. The verb is a reflexive stem (hithpael): they mixed *themselves*, an act they took part in, not something that merely happened to them. KJV's "were mingled" turns it passive and lets them off. BBE's "were joined to" does the same. "Learned" is the verb used for students and apprentices, and מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם, "their deeds", is the plain word for what people do, not a technical term for idolatry. The psalm leaves the content of those deeds unnamed here, and the next verses fill it in. Listen for the word again at v.39, where "their deeds" and "their doings" stand side by side, and the deeds learned from the nations have become Israel's own.

philological_notes.note: Hithpael of ערב, 'to mix'. The reflexive stem makes Israel the agent: they mixed themselves in. The same root gives the later Hebrew word for mixture, which Metzudat Zion hints at by tying it to תערובות ('mixtures').
'They learned', the verb of schooling and training, from the root that also gives 'goad' in the sense of teaching by prodding. Here the schooling is by daily contact, not by instruction.

verses.translation_literal: And they served their idols, and they became a snare for them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they served the idols of those nations, their idols of grief; and the idols became a trap to catch them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chain closes. The mixing becomes worship, and the worship becomes a trap. The word for "snare" is a trapper's term, a device that springs on its prey, and it is the very word used in Exodus 23:33, where serving the gods of the land is said to be a snare. The KJV "which were a snare unto them" is fine, but "idols" hides a barb: the Hebrew עצבים, from a root of "pain, hurt", is a taunt, "the hurtful things". Ibn Ezra says the word is used in contempt, and Metzudat Zion that the idol grieves the heart of its worshippers, who cry out and are not answered.

As with "sacrifices of the dead" in verse 28, the psalm is not neutral about the gods: they are things that hurt.

philological_notes.note: 'Idols', literally 'sorrows, hurtful things', a contemptuous name tied to the root meaning pain.
A snare or trap that catches the one who steps near it.

verses.translation_literal: And they sacrificed [obj] their sons and [obj] their daughters to the shedim.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, the unspeakable. They took their own sons, their own daughters, and laid them on the altars of the shedim.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the psalm's lowest point, and the Hebrew states it flatly: the same verb, זבח, that Israel used for a shared peace-offering meal is now used for children. Do not play it as a rant. Play it as a report, quiet and appalled. The word שֵׁדִים appears only here and in Deut 32:17 in the whole Bible; it is probably a loanword from Mesopotamia, where the šēdu was a guardian spirit that could turn dangerous. The psalmist's point is polemical: what Canaan treated as protective powers are nothing but 'shedim', lesser beings who are not God.

The KJV's 'devils' is a Christian-era word with Satan behind it, and it fits poorly: there is no Devil in the Hebrew here. Notice too that Hebrew names the daughters with their own 'et', a separate object marker, so that each group of children is counted. Child sacrifice is condemned in the law (Lev 18:21, Deut 12:31) and the prophets (Jer 7:31, Ezek 16:20-21), and it is the crime that, in this psalm's reckoning, turns the land itself against Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'To the shedim', a rare word found only here and in Deut 32:17, where it is also parallel to 'no-gods'. Probably cognate with Akkadian šēdu, a guardian spirit. Ibn Ezra reports an alternative derivation from שוד, 'devastate', which is also the basis for YLT's 'destroyers'.
The ordinary verb for sacrifice, used also for the shared meal offering. The ordinariness of the verb is what makes the object so shocking.

verses.translation_literal: And they shed blood, innocent, the blood of their sons and their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted by the bloods.
verses.translation_dramatic: They poured out innocent blood, the blood of their own sons and daughters, whom they gave to the idols of Canaan. And the land itself, soaked in it, grew foul beneath them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist now changes the legal category. Verse 37 said 'sacrifice'; verse 38 says 'shed innocent blood', the language of murder. Radak notes that besides idolatry they carry this second great guilt. The adjective נָקִי, 'innocent' or 'clean', is the same word used for someone cleared in court: these children had done nothing, and the verse makes the word land twice, once as an adjective and again in the repeated 'blood of'.

The last clause turns on the plural דָּמִים, 'bloods', the standard Hebrew plural for violently spilled blood (the KJV's flat 'blood' loses the plural of bloodshed). The verb וַתֶּחֱנַף, 'was polluted', is the verb of Num 35:33, where the law says that blood pollutes the land and only the blood of the one who shed it cleanses it. That is my own observation, not a packet citation. The land here is almost a character: it takes on the stain and will in time spit out its inhabitants. KJV 'idols of Canaan' is accurate enough, but עֲצַבִּים (from the root 'to shape, to hurt') are literally 'things made with pain', a sneer at man-made gods.

philological_notes.note: 'And it was polluted', said of the land. The same root appears in Num 35:33 for land defiled by bloodshed and in Jer 3:1-2 for land polluted by unfaithfulness. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'become guilty, become wicked'.
Plural 'bloods', the usual Hebrew form for blood shed in violence. Radak reads the definite article as pointing back to 'these bloods' just named.
'To the idols of'. The word is a pun on the root 'to shape' and 'to grieve': the idols are things shaped by hand that bring sorrow.

verses.translation_literal: And they became unclean by their works, and they played the prostitute by their deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: So they made themselves unclean with their own hands' work, and went whoring after their own devices.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs, one image: uncleanness (טמא), the cultic stain, and prostitution (זנה), the marriage metaphor the prophets use for Israel's unfaithfulness to its covenant husband. The 'works' and 'deeds' are not the idols but the people's own conduct. Malbim reads the two nouns differently: מעשים are the acts, מעללים the habits of soul behind them, so that the second word is worse, because the people have stopped doing evil and have become evil.

The KJV's 'went a whoring with their own inventions' keeps the harlotry but softens 'inventions', which suits the Hebrew מעללים only roughly: the word is used elsewhere simply for 'deeds, doings' (Jer 4:4, Mic 3:4), not 'inventions'. The Hebrew is more neutral and more damning for it: it is their own behavior that does the damage, not a foreign seduction. Radak finds sexual transgression behind זנה; Meiri and Metzudat David read it as a wider turning away from what is right. Both are possible, and the actors should choose the shame in the voice rather than the lewdness.

philological_notes.note: 'They played the prostitute', the prophetic verb for Israel's covenant unfaithfulness. Radak takes it as sexual sin; Metzudat Zion says it means 'turning aside', which is why a woman who strays from modesty is called a zonah.
'By their deeds'. Malbim distinguishes it from מעשים: these are the actions that flow from settled traits of character.

verses.translation_literal: And the nose of YHWH burned against his people, and he abhorred his inheritance.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the anger of the LORD blazed against his own people, and his own inheritance became an abomination to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns. Until now the people have acted; now God responds, and the verbs are the strongest of the book. 'The nose burned' is the Hebrew idiom for anger: the nostrils flare and heat, as in a bull or a man in a rage. KJV's 'wrath ... kindled' is a decent equivalent, but it converts a bodily image to an abstract one. The word אַף is literally 'nose', and the line asks the actor to let the breath show.

Then וַיְתָעֵב, 'he abhorred', from the root of תּוֹעֵבָה, 'abomination'. This is the word the law reserves for what is detestable to God: the very thing the people have done (v.37-38) now describes how God sees them. The irony is cutting. The word 'inheritance' (נַחֲלָה), as Malbim says, marks a bond of love and ownership, here turned into abomination. The KJV's 'insomuch that' reads a result into a plain 'and'. Meiri sees the pattern of the book of Judges: the people sin, God withdraws, over and over.

philological_notes.note: 'And he abhorred', from the root of 'abomination' (תּוֹעֵבָה). The verb turns the people's own category of abomination back on them. Metzudat Zion links it directly to תועבה.
'His inheritance', Israel as God's own property and family portion. Malbim says the word names a bond of love established through their holiness.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave them into the hand of nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.
verses.translation_dramatic: He handed them over, into the grip of the nations, and the ones who hated them became their masters.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the consequence, and it is told with a deliberate sound: the same verb, נתן, 'to give', that was God's gift of the land is now his giving of the people over. Rashi and Ibn Ezra place it in the era of the Judges, citing Eglon, Cushan-rishathaim, Sisera, the Philistines and Midian. The psalmist does not name them, and the verse should be played as a pattern, not a single event.

The KJV's 'heathen' is an archaism and carries a theological judgment the Hebrew גּוֹיִם does not, since גוי is simply 'nation'. Notice the noun ending: 'those who hated them', a participle. Hatred is the ruler. Malbim observes that the order of the verbs rises: first rule (משל), then oppression (לחץ, v.42), then submission. 'Hand' as a word for power runs through the verse and the next: the people fall from God's hand into the nations' hands, and the nations' hand will press down on them.

philological_notes.note: 'In the hand of', the Hebrew expression for power or control. The verse moves the people from one hand to another.
'Those who hated them', a participle with suffix. Malbim notes that the stages of subjugation worsen from 'haters' to 'enemies' (v.42).

verses.translation_literal: And their enemies oppressed them, and they were humbled under their hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their enemies pressed them down, harder and harder, until they bent, and bowed, and lay beneath their hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The next step down. לָחַץ, 'to squeeze, to press', is the verb of Egypt's oppression (Exod 3:9); the people who were once pressed in Egypt are pressed again. Then the Niphal of כנע, 'to be humbled, to be made to bow', which carries the image of someone forced to kneel. The KJV's 'brought into subjection' is correct in sense but formal; the Hebrew has the physical image of a body bending.

Ibn Ezra notes that the two clauses say nearly the same thing, which is intentional: the repetition has the weight of a blow struck twice. The 'hand' returns from v.41. Actors should feel the pressure slowly increasing and the voice sinking with it.

philological_notes.note: 'And they pressed them', the same verb used for the oppression in Egypt. Metzudat Zion relates it to pressure and constraint.
'They were humbled', a Niphal of כנע, literally 'made to bow down'. Ibn Ezra observes that the two halves of the verse repeat one meaning.

verses.translation_literal: Many times he delivered them, but they, they rebelled by their counsel, and they sank by their iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: Again and again he rescued them. And again and again they turned from him, hardened in their own plans, and sank into their own guilt.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pattern of the book of Judges compressed into one line (Judg 2:16-19, as Metzudat David and Malbim note). 'Many times' (פְּעָמִים רַבּוֹת) is one of the most important phrases in the psalm: God's patience is a cycle, and the Hebrew puts וְהֵמָּה, 'and they, they', as a sharp contrast with the pronoun spoken aloud. The grammar insists: He delivered; they rebelled.

The KJV's 'provoked him with their counsel' supplies 'him' (Radak confirms that it is God they defied) but the verb מָרָה, 'rebel, be bitter', is the word for stubborn defiance of authority, not 'provoke'. 'Counsel' (עֵצָה) is their own scheme, their own plan: Malbim says the rebellion was not driven by appetite but by deliberate thinking. The last verb וַיָּמֹכּוּ is rare: Rashi says 'they became low', Meiri and Ibn Ezra link it to the root of 'poor' (Lev 25:25), a pun on sinking. 'Iniquity' (עָוֺן) can mean both the crooked act and the guilt that follows it: the people sink into what they themselves made.

philological_notes.note: 'They rebelled', a Hiphil of מרה, to defy or be stubborn against authority. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'rebelled and refused'. Radak says the object, left unstated, is God.
'And they sank, were brought low'. Rashi glosses it 'were made low by their iniquity'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri connect it to מוך, 'to become poor' (Lev 25:25), or to מכך as a verb of sinking.
'By their counsel', their own plan. Malbim stresses that the rebellion was deliberate and reasoned, not impulsive.

verses.translation_literal: And he saw, in the distress to them, when he heard their ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet he saw them in their distress. He heard their crying out, and he did not look away.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn of the whole psalm, and it is the shortest, plainest line in the passage. After the long list of rebellion, the Hebrew gives two simple verbs: he saw, he heard. Compare Exod 2:24-25, where the same pair begins the Exodus. The KJV's 'Nevertheless he regarded their affliction' supplies a 'nevertheless' the Hebrew does not have: the verse begins with a simple 'and', and its force comes from the silence before it.

רִנָּה is a loud, ringing sound: it can be a shout of joy or, as here, a shout of anguish (Ibn Ezra glosses it 'outcry', comparing 'the cry passed through the camp' in 1 Kgs 22:36). The KJV's 'cry' is fine. 'Distress' (צַר) literally means 'narrow', a tight place, and the same root as 'enemy' (צר): trouble and the one who causes it share a word. Rashi says the hearing was by virtue of prayer and then, in a second comment, by the merit of the fathers. Actors should play God here as a listener first.

philological_notes.note: 'Their ringing cry'. Usually a shout of joy, but here a cry of entreaty. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'their outcry'.
'In the distress', literally 'in the narrowness'. Rashi says God saw 'from within prayer'.

verses.translation_literal: And he remembered for them his covenant, and he relented according to the greatness of his covenant loyalties.
verses.translation_dramatic: He remembered his covenant, for their sake, and he softened, as his great and faithful love bade him.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Remember' in Hebrew is not recall but action: God remembered means God acted on the promise (Gen 8:1, Exod 2:24). The covenant here is, per Radak and Metzudat David, the one with the fathers (Lev 26:44-45); Ibn Ezra argues for Sinai instead. The text does not decide, and the director should not either.

The KJV's 'repented' for וַיִּנָּחֶם is the most misleading word in the verse: the verb means 'to be moved to compassion, to relent', and it does not imply that God did wrong. The KJV here is archaic and, to a modern ear, theologically wrong. Radak says the relenting is 'from the evil', that is, from the punishment. The last phrase, 'the greatness of his חֲסָדִים', is the key: חֶסֶד is covenant loyalty, steadfast love that holds a bond. The text as written has the singular חסדו, but the traditional reading is the plural 'loyalties', a plurality of acts of love. Metzudat David notes the contrast: God acts by his love, not by what they deserve.

philological_notes.note: 'He relented'. A Niphal of נחם: to be moved to pity and change course. KJV 'repented' misleads in modern English. Radak and Metzudat David both gloss it 'from the evil', that is the threatened punishment.
Written (Ketiv) as the singular חסדו, 'his loyalty', and read (Qere) as the plural 'his loyalties'. Covenant love: faithfulness within a relationship, not a general 'mercy' as in KJV.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave them [obj] into compassions before all their captors.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he put tenderness in the hearts of those who held them, so that even their captors looked on them with pity.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb נתן, 'give', returns for the third time: God gave them over to the nations (v.41), and now he gives them into compassions. The same hand that handed them over now softens the hand that holds them. The Hebrew is spare: 'he gave them to compassions before all their captors', a construction the KJV smooths into 'he made them to be pitied'. It reads as a small mercy: not freedom, only that the captor does not crush.

רַחֲמִים is a plural abstract, from רֶחֶם, 'womb': compassion in its bodily, maternal sense. The plural sits with the plural חֲסָדִים of the previous verse. Radak and Metzudat David read it as the captors' pity, so that the burden was not made heavy; Meiri connects it to the later exiles. A reference to 1 Kgs 8:50 and 2 Chr 30:9 is likely, but it is my own association. Notice the quiet note: the captors, שֹׁבֵיהֶם, are those who 'took captive', a participle of שבה, which puts the exile in the frame.

philological_notes.note: 'Into compassions'. Plural of the abstract; the root is the word for 'womb', so the sense is a tender, almost maternal feeling. Radak and Metzudat David read it as the captors' pity.
'Their captors', a participle of שבה, 'to take captive'. Metzudat Zion links it to שביה, captivity.

verses.translation_literal: Save us, YHWH our God, and gather us from the nations, to give thanks to the name of your holiness, to glory in your praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Save us, LORD our God. Save us, and gather us in from among the nations, from every far place where we were scattered, so that our mouths may be free to give thanks to your holy name, and our voices may rise and glory in your praise.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a change of voice. The 'we' is not new: it came in at verse 6 with "we have sinned with our fathers," and it has carried the whole long history of Israel's failures since. Until now that 'we' confessed. Here it asks. Two imperatives come first, "Save us" and "gather us," and the singer leans on them with the title "YHWH our God," the covenant name joined to a possessive. The cry follows verse 46, where even captors were made to pity. The one who made that happen is now asked to finish it. The people are still in exile, and the request is to be brought home.

The KJV's "from among the heathen" adds "among" and a word that nowhere appears here. The Hebrew says only "from the nations" (min-hagoyim), a plain geographic and political term. "Heathen" gives it an English colouring of contempt. The KJV's "triumph in thy praise" is also too martial: lehishtabeach is a reflexive form (to glory, to boast) and the thing glorified in is praise itself. The prayer does not ask for rescue so that Israel can be safe. It asks for rescue so that Israel can give thanks and praise: the purpose clauses are the point. Note too the name of "holiness" (shem qodshekha), literally 'name of your holiness,' a construct chain the KJV smooths into the adjective "holy name." Traditional commentators hear this as the voice of the exiles (Radak, Ibn Ezra). Whoever stands behind it, the verse sits at the very end of Book IV, and the next verse is the book's closing blessing.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of yasha', 'to save, to deliver,' with 'us.' The root means to bring into open space out of constriction. It is the same root as 'Hosanna', which is hoshi'a na, 'save, please.' Rashi reads it as 'also now', asking for what was done before to be done again.

Piel imperative of qabatz, 'to gather,' with 'us.' It is the verb of regathering the scattered, as in the promise of Deuteronomy 30:3-4 that Malbim cites: 'and he will return and gather you from all the peoples.'

Hithpael infinitive of shabach: 'to glory, to boast, to declare oneself praised.' It is reflexive in form. KJV 'triumph' is too martial, STEPBible 'boast' too self-regarding. The praise is God's, and the people take their glory in it.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] YHWH, God of Israel, from the age and until the age. And let all the people say: Amen. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from age to age, forever. And let all the people say: Amen! Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The doxology that closes the fourth book of the Psalter (compare Pss 41:14, 72:18-19, 89:53). The shape is the stage direction of a liturgy: the leader blesses, the whole congregation answers 'Amen', and everyone shouts 'Hallelujah' (Ibn Ezra notes the psalm ends as it began, with that word). Radak adds that the wise will praise according to their understanding and all the people will say Amen. Metzudat David reads it as an invitation to those who do not know how to bless: 'Praise, you who know how'.

The KJV's 'from everlasting to everlasting' is a fair translation of the idiom, though the Hebrew מִן־הָעוֹלָם וְעַד הָעוֹלָם is literally 'from the age to the age', and Rashi reads it, citing Sanhedrin 92a, as 'from this world to the world to come'. אָמֵן comes from the root for 'firm, trustworthy': the people say, 'it is so, let it be so'. The KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' turns הַלְלוּ־יָהּ, 'Praise Yah', into English and hides the short divine name Yah; modern readers should hear that the name stays inside the shout.

philological_notes.note: 'From the age to the age', the Hebrew idiom for always. Rashi, citing Sanhedrin 92a, reads it as from this world to the world to come; Metzudat David and Radak read it as from the beginning to the end of time.
'Amen', from the root for firmness and trust. Ibn Ezra derives it from אמונה, 'faithfulness'. Metzudat David says it means: the matter is true.
'Praise Yah', a plural imperative with the short form of the divine name. Ibn Ezra notes that the psalm closes with the same word that opened it.
